entries.title: EP230: RAG vs Agentic RAG
entries.summary: Here's how RAG and agentic RAG typically work.
entries.content:

This week’s system design refresher:

  • Top 5 AI Building Blocks Every Engineer Should Know (Youtube Video)

  • RAG vs Agentic RAG

  • OAuth (authorization) + OIDC (authentication layer)

  • Understanding the Linux Directory Structure

Top 5 AI Building Blocks Every Engineer Should Know

RAG vs Agentic RAG

RAG is a technique that combines information retrieval with an LLM to generate answers. Here is how RAG works at a high level:

  • A user asks a question to the application.

  • The retrieval system fetches the relevant information from a knowledge base.

  • The application adds that information to the prompt.

  • The LLM uses that context to generate an answer.

RAG usually follows a predefined retrieval process. The quality of its results depends on the accuracy of the retrieved context.

Agentic RAG follows a different approach. Instead of retrieving once, an agent can repeatedly fetch and evaluate information until it has enough evidence to generate an answer. Here is how it typically works:

  • An agent selects the right tools based on the task.

  • Those tools can search documents, APIs, databases, or the web.

  • The fetched evidence is then checked if it is sufficient for the task.

  • If it is not, the agent can adjust its search or choose a different tool.

  • Once sufficient evidence is achieved, LLM uses that context to generate an answer.

Thank You, Open Source Maintainers (Sponsored)

Open source is the foundation of nearly everything we build, and the maintainers behind it make it possible. The good news: the movement to support them is growing.

Two years ago, the Open Source Pledge set out to make paying maintainers the norm. Today, 37 member companies have paid $8.4M to maintainers and foundations, and every new member adds to that momentum.

See how Sentry put $1M to work this year, or join the Pledge and be part of what’s next.

OAuth (authorization) + OIDC (authentication layer)

If you want to show Google Calendar events inside your Slack channel, it will require permission to read your calendar. How would you let Slack access your calendar without giving Slack your Google password?

This is where OAuth 2.0 comes into the picture. Slack basically never sees your Google password. It lets an app access a protected resource on your behalf without knowing your credentials.

Basically OAuth 2.0 handles authorization. In Slack’s case, it will send you to Google’s authorization server, where you will login and give Slack permission to access your calendar. Google gives you the authorization code, and Slack will exchange that code for access_token.

If Slack also wants to authenticate the identity of the person requesting the access to Google Calendar, you will need OIDC for that. The OIDC handles authentication and sits on top of OAuth 2.0.

OAuth answers what you’re allowed to touch, while OIDC answers who you are. In addition to the access_token returned by the authorization server, this time, it will also send an id_token, a signed JWT which basically tells Slack who just signed in.

Understanding the Linux Directory Structure

The linux directory structure starts with the root directory "/". Let’s navigate to the directory structure of linux.

The kernel image and bootloader files are stored in the "boot" directory. Your hard disk partitions and device related files are located in the “dev” directory.

All your programs and libraries are stored in "bin", "sbin", "usr", and "lib" directories. Like, your installed software is located in the "usr" directory. Ever wondered where ls, cp, and cat commands are? "bin" is the directory that holds those essential commands.

System-wide configuration goes in "etc", and "var" holds data that changes as the system runs, which is where you'll find your logs.

If you have a USB drive, it gets mounted in “bin” folder. For any external drive that you want to mount temporarily on your linux machine, "media" is the directory for it. If you have multiple user accounts, "home" is the directory for each user in your linux system.

entries.title: Why Distributed Systems Prefer Independence over Coordination
entries.summary: In this article, we’ll look at why coordination is a challenge for distributed systems.
entries.content:
In a distributed system, you have components running in separate processes or machines. These components could be application services, database replicas, or even background workers.

Since in distributed systems, we divide the system into so many components, it’s pretty common that one component may need to talk to another component to get something done. It may also have to wait for the other component’s response. You can think of coordination as this talking between components. For example, you may have one service waiting for another service to approve a request. Or a database waits for acknowledgment from its replicas. Or a worker waits for a lock.

In this article, we’ll look at why coordination is a challenge for distributed systems. Here’s what we will cover.

  • Why coordination becomes a challenge

  • How coordination increases in a system

  • How to reduce coordination

  • Strategies to handle coordination

entries.title: LLM Prompt Caching Versus Semantic Caching
entries.summary: In this article, we’ll look at how LLM caching works in detail.
entries.content:

Caching is a super important aspect of system design, especially for large-scale systems. You can use a cache to store some data that is expensive to calculate so that it can be reused later without paying the same cost. For example, a website might cache the result of a database query instead of running that query every time someone opens a page.

The same is the case for large language models. Just like normal systems, caching in LLM applications also means storing stuff calculated as part of earlier requests so that we can reuse it later. This helps bring down processing costs and response time, especially when requests contain the same instructions, documents, or questions.

However, there are two types of ways we can cache stuff in LLMs: prompt caching and semantic caching. Both have the same general aim of reducing repeated work, but they work at different stages of a request. They also follow different rules.

In this article, we’ll look at how LLM caching works in detail. Here’s what you’ll learn:

  • Why an LLM request costs money

  • What is prompt caching

  • Where to place the shared content in prompt caching

  • What is semantic caching

  • The difficulty with semantic caching

  • Why checking the question is not enough

  • When to invalidate the cache

  • How prompt and semantic caching can work together

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

Why an LLM Request Costs Money

When you send some text to an LLM, the LLM processes that text and generates a response. During processing, the text is divided into tokens. Each token is a small piece of text. A token can be a word, part of a word, or punctuation.

These tokens directly impact the cost. For a typical text-generation API, the cost has two main components:

  • The tokens provided as input.

  • The tokens generated as output.

Output tokens often cost more for obvious reasons. However, the input tokens can also cost a lot because of the size. Input can include much more than just the user’s latest question. For example, let’s say you have a customer-support application. Along with the current question, this application can also send a bunch of instructions telling the model how it should behave. It might also send examples of good answers. Relevant product documentation. Earlier conversation messages. In other words, a 10-word question can be part of a request made up of 1000s of input tokens.

Let’s say you have another application that sends a long product manual with every user request. This product manual is like an encyclopedia of all the information that the user might be looking for. One user might ask about the installation procedure. Another asks about troubleshooting. Maybe a third user asks about account settings. While their questions happen to be different, the answers are all there in the same long product manual that is part of every request.

There is another type of repetition as well. 100s of users might ask how to change their profile picture. But each user might write the query using slightly different words. In such a case, the model may end up generating the same rough answer again and again.

As you can notice, we have two opportunities to reduce this repetitive work and bring down costs:

  • What if the application can reuse the input information that has already been processed once? For example, the product manual.

  • What if the application can reuse a previously generated answer if it is suitable? For example, similar questions asked again and again.

Prompt caching is used to exploit the first opportunity. Semantic caching is for the second one. Let’s look at both in detail.

Prompt Caching: Reusing the Model’s Input Processing

To make caching effective, you need a rule to decide whether something is fit for reuse. This rule is the most important part of building an effective cache setup.

For prompt caching, the rule is to match the beginning of the model’s input.

A typical text-generating transformer model works in two stages:

  • First, it processes the input. This stage is called prefill.

  • Second, it generates new tokens. This stage is called decoding.

When processing the input, the model converts text to numbers. This numeric representation helps the model use information it read earlier to generate output tokens down the line. Some of these representations are called keys and values. Or KV states.

Keys help the attention mechanism find out which earlier information is useful. Values are the actual representations of that information. A KV cache stores these intermediate results so that they can be reused. This is all part of the ordinary text generation flow in an LLM.

Prompt caching piggybacks on this reuse setup. It extends the whole thing for all the compatible input requests that share the same beginning. Let’s say you have the following two requests:

Request A: Support instructions + product manual + “How is installation configured?”

Request B: Support instructions + product manual + “How are diagnostic logs enabled?”

As you can see, the support instructions and the product manual are shared across both requests. They are known as the shared prefix. The actual question is part of the suffix that keeps changing for each input request.

After the model processes Request A, the system can store the KV states for the shared prefix. When Request B arrives, the model can reuse those same KV states to process the new question and generate the answer. We’ve reused the intermediate computation for the common context. No recalculation. No reprocessing.

Where to Place the Shared Content in Prompt Caching

For prompt caching to work, we need to put the shared content at the beginning of the request. Basically, the prefix position. The word “prefix” is important here because a token’s internal representation depends on the information that comes before it in the input.

In a typical causal language model, the tokens that come earlier in the prompt can’t look forward at the question that might appear later in the request. This is why a model can reuse the shared stuff from the beginning even when the final user question is completely different.

However, when you place a different question before the manual, it changes the way the manual is processed. The question impacts the representation of the text in the manual. The manual’s text is the same. But the processed version is completely different.

This is the reason we have to place fixed, stable instructions or any shared reference material before the request details that can change. Even if you place a seemingly unimportant timestamp or random request ID at the beginning of the input, it can stop the model from reusing a large chunk of shared stuff.

To be clear, even the instructions need to be “exactly” similar. Even if you have two instructions that might mean the same thing, you cannot use them interchangeably for prompt caching. There should be no change in wording. No change in document order. No change in request settings.

The Cost Savings from Prompt Caching

Simply caching the shared prefix doesn’t make the cost zero. Most LLM providers usually charge it at a discounted rate. Also, the output token charges stay the same because the model still generates a fresh answer.

For reference, Anthropic’s standard prompt-cache pricing uses a cache-read rate of 1/10th of the ordinary input rate. There are some exceptions for particular models. Its standard 5-minute cache write costs 1.25 times the ordinary input rate, while a 1-hour write costs twice that rate. These are total rates for the affected tokens, rather than additional charges on top of their ordinary input cost.

As an example, if processing a prefix normally costs $1, that five-minute pricing schedule makes the initial write cost $1.25 and a subsequent read cost $0.10. Therefore, one write followed by one read costs $1.35 instead of $2. The more the number of reads, the greater the savings. But if a cached prefix is never reused, you don’t get any benefit.

LLM provider and model rules also determine minimum eligible lengths, expiration, and cache-write pricing. Even if we repeat a prompt, it doesn’t guarantee a cache hit if the cache record has expired or is unavailable.

To summarize, prompt caching mainly reduces input-processing work and can reduce the wait time before we generate a response. You cannot use it to eliminate the work that goes into generating a long answer.

Semantic Caching: Reusing a Previous Answer

Semantic caching is usually part of the application that surrounds an LLM. It can also be a separate service that the application calls before it goes to the LLM for an answer. Consider a couple of example questions that you might ask an LLM:

“Where is the setting for dark mode?”

“How can I switch the app to its dark theme?”

As you can notice, the same answer may be able to satisfy both questions if there’s no change to the application features in a major way. But a simple text comparison would consider them as two separate questions with two different answers. However, a semantic comparison can identify that they are essentially the same query asked in slightly different words.

To implement semantic caching, you need an embedding model. This type of model converts text into a list of numbers called a vector. These numbers represent features of the text in a way that makes it easy to compare two pieces of text.

The overall flow works as follows:

  • The embedding model creates an embedding for the incoming question.

  • It searches question embeddings that are already stored for suitable candidate answers.

  • It checks whether a candidate answer is similar and valid for the current question.

  • If accepted, it returns the stored answer. Basically, a cache hit.

  • On a miss, it calls the LLM to generate a fresh answer. It may store the answer for future reuse.

As you can see, if there’s a cache hit, we don’t have to call the LLM to generate a fresh answer. No input and output charges in that case. However, tasks like embedding generation, lookup, and cache storage still use resources. So it’s not all free. Also, if we have a cache miss, we pay for the preliminary tasks as well as the LLM request. So a miss ends up being more costly.

The Difficulty With Semantic Caching

The most difficult part with semantic caching is to find out how similar two separate questions are.

In a semantic cache, we calculate a similarity score and compare it to some threshold. You can think of this threshold like a cutoff for accepting that the questions are similar.

If we keep a very strict threshold, we end up rejecting many more answer candidates. While this can improve accuracy and reduce inappropriate reuse, it also rejects a lot of legitimate paraphrases of the question. However, if we go for a loose threshold, more answer candidates get accepted. This increases the overall cache hit rate. But it also increases the possibility of returning an unsuitable answer. There is no single, universal threshold that works perfectly for every application. You need to decide the threshold on a case-by-case basis.

Let’s say a user asks two questions about cancelling an order before it gets shipped and after it gets shipped.

As you can see, both questions are almost the same. Except for one critical word that changes the meaning. Both questions deal with cancellation and shipping. Their embeddings may also be quite close. But a short answer of “Yes, cancellation is available” could be the correct answer for one, but totally incorrect for the other.

Data types like numbers, negation, dates, product editions, and eligibility conditions can cause similar problems while determining similarity. For example, “Does the Basic plan include backups?” cannot automatically reuse the answer to a question about the Pro plan.

Also, we cannot consider a similarity score the same as the probability of an answer being correct. For example, even if you get a similarity score of 0.92 between two questions, it doesn’t mean there is a 92% chance that the cached answer is suitable for both. The way we interpret the score depends on the embedding model and comparison method. Some systems expose a distance score instead, in which smaller values indicate closer matches.

Therefore, we need to have an evaluation process to find out the effectiveness of a semantic caching implementation. This evaluation process has to find out if a particular stored answer can satisfy a new request correctly. For testing purposes, the development team can collect a bunch of requests, identify candidate answers, and label whether reusing a specific answer is the right way. The test suite should have examples that cover legitimate paraphrases as well as difficult near-matches. This way, we have a better chance to find out the optimal threshold value.

Lastly, we need to measure the proportion of requests answered from cache and the proportion of those answers that are actually appropriate. We cannot celebrate just by achieving a high hit rate. We can also have an additional verifier that checks border cases. However, such a verifier also contributes to costs and latency.

Why We Can’t Rely On Just Checking the Question

You can ask the same question multiple times. But every time, you might expect a different answer. For example, a question like “What is my order status?” depends on the customer and the current status of the order. Similarly, a question such as “Does it support offline access?” depends on what the word “it” means in the conversation’s context. Also, if the user requests an answer in a different language, we can’t automatically respond with a cached answer generated in English.

Therefore, for a semantic cache to work, we need information beyond just the question to make the right decisions. Depending on the application’s use case, we may need to include stuff about the customer or organization, access permissions, product version, language, relevant conversation state, and source-data version.

Also, we need to enforce these conditions as part of the application. You cannot expect an embedding model to find the details of a customer just because the user included a customer identifier in the input question. Typically, semantic-cache implementations need to have metadata filters so that searches can be restricted to an appropriate scope.

There is another example that shows a specific complication. If the user asks questions such as “What’s the weather in NYC?” and “NYC weather today?”, they might look like suitable matches. But their answers depend on whether the user is looking for current conditions or a daily forecast. While generating an answer, we need to consider location, date, forecast period, units, and freshness.

When To Invalidate the Cache

There are chances that a cached answer might appear like an excellent match for a new question. But the answer might still be wrong because the source information behind the answer may have changed.

Let’s say you have an application that allowed product returns to take place within 30 days. Now the company has changed the policy. The product return time period has been reduced to 14 days. However, a cached answer might still talk about the old time period of 30 days. In this case, you might ask the same question and get the cached answer, which is no longer valid.

This is why we need to have a strategy for invalidating the cache.

Invalidation means making a cache entry unavailable for reuse. We can use multiple approaches to build an ideal invalidation setup.

The first approach is to define a TTL value. A TTL (time-to-live) adds an expiration time to a cached record. Deciding the TTL value is the key. If we keep a short TTL, we place a strong limit on how long stale information can stay eligible within the system. But there is still some gap that will always remain. TTL cannot guarantee freshness of data before expiration. For example, if a policy changes immediately after an answer is cached, that answer can be stale till the TTL expires.

The second approach is to use versioning. You can allow reuse of data based on a specific version. For example, an answer cached under policy_version=12 is ineligible when the application expects version 13.

It’s much easier to have a version that contains the entire knowledge base. But there’s a disadvantage. One small update can make the entire knowledge base invalid. All the cached answers are suddenly stale. However, if we invalidate only those things that have changed, it’s much more efficient. Much more selective. But to make it work, we need to track which answers depend on which documents or records.

The third approach that can impact cache invalidation is the overall settings we have used to generate answers. Things like high-level instructions. Output formats. Model behaviour guidelines. And so on. These settings matter a lot when deciding when to invalidate a cache. If these settings are changed, we should invalidate the earlier answers.

Invalidating a prompt cache is different from its cousin. If the application sends an updated policy in the prompt, the modified prefix cannot reuse an incompatible old version from the point at which the policy changed. However, if there is an unchanged earlier portion, it might still be reusable. Also, if the application keeps providing the old policy as part of every input, prompt caching cannot automatically find out if the actual business rule has changed somewhere. It’s the application’s responsibility to fetch the current policy information and feed it to the model.

Can Prompt and Semantic Caching Work Together

You can use prompt caching and semantic caching in the same setup. They are complementary. For example, you can have the application first look for a valid existing answer using semantic caching. If no such answer is available, only then does the application call the LLM and take advantage of any reusable prompt prefix.

If we get a semantic-cache hit, we don’t need to go for the main generation request. On the other hand, prompt caching reduces the cost of requests that still reach the LLM. We can also have an exact-answer cache that is checked before any semantic lookup happens. It can handle repeated identical requests cheaply.

It’s not necessary that we have a cache lookup at the very beginning of the flow. For example, if the application must retrieve current source versions to validate an answer, that particular check should happen even earlier.

Conclusion

Prompt caching is a natural choice in scenarios where you need to generate fresh answers for different questions. But those answers have to be generated from a shared context. This common context could be a general product manual, a set of instructions, stable tool definitions, or a long conversation history.

Semantic caching is great for cases where the same answer is good enough for many different requests. For example, product FAQs. Stable support instructions. However, semantic caching doesn’t work well when you want to generate highly personalized answers. Or if the answer depends on rapidly changing facts. Also, when there is a need for fresh creative output.

We need to have even greater care for action requests. For example, a cached message saying “The subscription has been cancelled” cannot be a substitute for making a real cancellation.

For a practical implementation of these caching strategies, we need to have some measurements. In the case of prompt caching, we need to measure how many input tokens are reused. This is because there is a major cost difference between serving a request that reuses a tiny prefix and one that reuses a long manual. For semantic caching, we need to evaluate metrics like accepted answers, freshness, and scope. Only those answers that satisfy the application’s quality requirements should be turned into reusable entries.

The ultimate goal with either approach is to lower cost and provide faster responses while preserving answer quality.

entries.title: Why Shopify Migrated From React Native
entries.summary: In this article, we’ll look at how Shopify decided to move out of React Native and how they migrated to native mobile development.
entries.content:
Stop scrubbing through session replays (Sponsored)

Most teams record session replays at a flat sample rate, then spend the next incident scrolling through hundreds of sessions that have nothing to do with the bug.

This hands-on Sentry workshop shows you how to capture the replays that matter:

  • Sample rates and buffer mode, plus the default we recommend

  • Custom React hooks to record a specific user segment, a known-bad URL, or a flow you just shipped

  • Bug reports that arrive with the replay already attached

  • Filters for rage clicks, dead clicks, and custom tags

  • Privacy defaults and how to tune them

In 2020, the Shopify engineering team decided to go all in on React Native. It saved them a ton of time and money. By using React Native, the developers didn’t have to implement the same feature in both Kotlin and Swift to make it work on Android and iOS. Sure, the framework came with its requirements. But the idea was very successful at the time.

However, in 2026, AI coding agents have made a huge difference to the economics of building mobile apps. Earlier, if you implemented something with React Native, you could justify the savings that came because of it. But now, AI agents have become so good at coding that building the same feature in Swift and Kotlin is much cheaper.

In this article, we’ll look at how Shopify decided to move out of React Native and how they migrated to native mobile development. Here’s what we’ll cover:

  • What is native mobile development

  • Why Shopify chose React Native

  • What changed in 2025

  • Shopify’s migration approach

  • How Shopify ran the migration

  • The agent feedback loop

  • The migration results

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

What is Native Mobile Development

As you might be aware, an iPhone runs Apple’s iOS, and Android phones run Android. Both these OS provide a bunch of facilities to display the UI, handle notifications, and talk to the device hardware.

In native mobile development for a particular OS, you build an application directly using the languages, frameworks, and tools for that platform. This means Swift for iOS and Kotlin for Android. To be clear, a programming language is different from a UI framework. For example, Swift and Kotlin are programming languages. However, Apple’s SwiftUI and Android’s Jetpack Compose are frameworks. These frameworks give developers the tools to create the real UI with various components like text, buttons, lists, layouts, and animations.

To build natively for both platforms, you need to maintain two implementations of the mobile application. One for Android. Another for iOS. Sure, you can share the backend services for both platforms, but the client code will still be separate.

However, React Native lets you share much of that implementation across both iOS and Android. It’s a framework for building mobile apps using React and JavaScript (or TypeScript). The main benefit of React Native is that many components and application code you write using this framework can work with both iOS and Android. You don’t need to implement every screen independently in Swift and Kotlin. This is because React Native sits on top of the native UI components that are backed by their respective platforms. For example, if you make a component in React Native, it can create the appropriate iOS or Android views without the need for developers to write any platform-specific code.

To be clear, sharing code doesn’t mean that every platform difference is completely gone. You would still have some features that might need platform-specific coding. Also, you need to build, test, and release the application for each OS.

[Webinar] How to stop rewriting your agent’s code (Sponsored)

Right now, you’re your agent’s context engine. You write the rules files, maintain the skills, and paste in the Slack thread it missed.

But hand-curated context goes stale. And when there are conflicting answers, your agent can’t tell which is right. You pay for it in higher token bills and longer reviews.

Join us live on Oct 28 (FREE) to see:

  • The 8-levels of AI maturity and where teams get stuck

  • How a context engine curates context and resolves conflicts before your agent writes a line of code

  • Live demo: token savings in the same coding task, and use cases beyond code gen

Bonus: 2 open source tools you can use today.

Why Shopify Went With React Native

The Shopify engineering team went with React Native in 2020. They wanted to solve three problems that were more or less linked.

The first problem was that you had to implement every feature two times with native development. One time for each platform. The second was that you couldn’t share developers between platforms. A developer was confined to their tech stack. An iOS developer couldn’t work on the Android version. Neither could the Android developer work on the iOS version. Not a great way to utilize the developers in a team.

The third problem was that you had to maintain feature parity across both versions. Feature parity is when every version of the app has the same features and capabilities. Let’s say, if you have a cool feature that works on iOS, but it takes another month to be available on Android, you can say that the two versions are out of parity. If you don’t maintain this parity, you risk alienating the user base of the platform that usually runs behind.

Also, when you have two versions of the app, you need to change both versions whenever there’s a change in any requirements. Even if the change is something as small as a text change. As you can see, this is a continuous cost problem that is present throughout the life of the application. You also need to have more coordination between the different platform teams while planning releases, announcements, and so on.

By going with React Native, Shopify reduced the impact of these problems in a big way. No need to implement every feature twice. No need to coordinate changes across multiple platform teams. It also made mobile development easy for developers already familiar with React and TypeScript. This is great because you could easily move people between projects. Plus, you also get to select developers from a much bigger TypeScript or JavaScript talent pool.

What Changed in 2025

As a framework, React Native has a lot of benefits. We have seen that already in the earlier section. But the framework also needs maintenance. This means additional costs.

The Shopify engineering team had to spend effort on optimizing the framework’s performance. They made improvements to the React Native foundations and contributed to framework upgrades. They also had to deal with changes to external dependencies. You can think of a dependency as a piece of software that the application relies on. If there’s a change in the dependency, you need to make changes to the application as well.

Native development is different from using a framework. The application has greater synergy with the platform and first-party tooling. You can use the tools provided by the platform’s own developers. Also, you have fewer dependency layers between the application code and the platform (iOS or Android).

Shopify was already using native code for some features. For example, widgets and watch applications. Also, for some background processing. You could say that React Native and native development coexisted within the application for several years. Of course, the benefit equation tilted more towards React Native.

However, the rise of coding agents made big changes to the equation. As you know, a large language model (LLM) can generate code quite easily. A coding agent combines an LLM with special tools that can read code files, edit code, and run tests. It could also check why things are failing and make changes to handle those failures.

By 2025, these agents had improved so much that Shopify had to take another look at its mobile strategy. To test the waters, the Shopify engineering team rebuilt some core parts of its application in Swift and Kotlin. These prototypes proved that the coding agents could take an implementation on one platform as a reference and write the equivalent code for the other platform.

For example, you can have an iOS feature that provides all the details about the UI elements, actions, and error conditions. An agent can use those details and build an Android equivalent. Sure, developers had to check whether the outcome was good enough and followed the conventions of Android and the overall architecture. However, suddenly, you had developers who could use these agents to code stuff outside their primary stack without a lot of effort.

Of course, with native development, two implementations would still be there. Both will need to be maintained. But Shopify claims that coding agents have reduced the work to such a level that concerns about duplication are no longer as important for making decisions as they were in 2020.

Shopify’s Migration Approach

To carry out the migration to native, Shopify had to choose the best pathway to migrate the existing applications. You have two ways to do so.

First, we have brownfield migration. In this approach, you change an existing application gradually. New and old implementations run together as individual parts are replaced. While the risk is lower, the migration takes more time. Also, you have to manage the integration between the new and old implementations.

Second, we have a greenfield approach. In this approach, you create a fresh implementation. Developers get more freedom to design a new architecture. However, you need to build an almost complete replacement before getting rid of the existing product. There’s no incremental change.

Shopify had used the brownfield approach earlier for some of its large applications. The development methods at the time would have taken too long. However, when they tried the new prototypes, the team found out that a fresh native implementation would be faster. The existing React Native application was a solid reference point for how things should work.

Therefore, Shopify chose the greenfield approach.

They first shipped the Shop app. This app was used by shoppers. The larger Shopify app, which is used by merchants, was migrated later. For reference, the Shopify app has more than 300 screens. Also, many features, such as widgets. And an Apple Watch application.

How Shopify Ran the Migration

When planning the migration, the Shopify engineering team found that if you asked a model to rebuild a large feature in one attempt, you got mediocre results. The output code was difficult to maintain. Also, it was very difficult for developers to properly review big features.

Therefore, Shopify built Helix to support the migration. Helix breaks the migration into small steps that can be reviewed. With Helix, you can have a developer select a screen, and Helix proposes small pieces of migration in the best possible order. Each migration piece has to go through the review process. Only then does it become the foundation for the next piece.

For example, let’s say you have an order detail screen. An initial checkpoint can finalize the structure of the screen and how navigation should work. Later checkpoints will deal with other features such as order summary and customer information. Each checkpoint is small enough that developers can review it properly.

Four types of checks are done to make sure everything works as intended.

First, you have the behavioural tests. You take expected actions on the app and check what happens. Second, you have the visual review. In this, we check how the new UI looks compared with the old reference application.

Next, you have adversarial code reviews. Two reviewers look for problems in the code. They try to find issues that might stay hidden behind a normal workflow. Lastly, we have another developer review where we check the results of the previous tests. If everything meets expectations, things proceed further.

The best part about Helix is that the team gets continuous feedback while the change is still small.

The Agent Feedback Loop

Shopify has a design philosophy that separates app logic from the UI.

For example, you can have a form with rules about valid or invalid inputs. To test them, you don’t need a visible text box. They can receive an input value and return a result.

Shopify’s architectural principle is to keep the business logic independent of the UI. The idea is that the business logic can run headlessly. You can expose the application state and actions through a CLI. This way, the agents can check state, navigate between sections, and perform actions.

While navigating like this without a UI might sound strange, it makes it easy to check how things work. You can have an agent take an action and check the state. There’s no need to make sense of screenshots and find out where a button is located. This is why behavioural checks can be made quite fast.

The Migration Results

The Shop app was live on the app stores as a native application in 12 weeks. There were many interesting stats.

The app startup time on iOS went down from 3200 ms on React Native to approximately 2400 ms on the Native version. The startup time on Android had even greater gains, going from around 4400 ms to 2200 ms. Almost half. The crash-free sessions went up. Also, the app size on Android was down from 293 MB for React Native to 184 MB for the native version.

All in all, these results have been quite encouraging for the Shopify engineering team. Of course, their approach combines a lot of things that make it successful. For starters, you have direct use of platform tech. You also have an existing application, which can act as a strong reference point. Also, the migration process is made smooth with small implementation checkpoints and quality checks.

The main thing we can take away from Shopify’s case is to have a fast feedback loop that can check if the code generated by AI agents is good enough. This is the key to making big migrations like this safe for the users.

entries.title: How Uber Built a Genie to Answer Questions Correctly
entries.summary: In this article, we will understand how Genie prepares knowledge, retrieves it, and generates answers.
entries.content:
[Webinar] How to stop rewriting your agent’s code (Sponsored)

Right now, you’re your agent’s context engine. You write the rules files, maintain the skills, and paste in the Slack thread it missed.

But hand-curated context goes stale. And when there are conflicting answers, your agent can’t tell which is right. You pay for it in higher token bills and longer reviews.

Join us live on Oct 28 (FREE) to see:

  • The 8-levels of AI maturity and where teams get stuck

  • How a context engine curates context and resolves conflicts before your agent writes a line of code

  • Live demo: token savings in the same coding task, and use cases beyond code gen

Bonus: 2 open source tools you can use today.

Genie is Uber’s internal AI assistant for answering engineering support questions. It finds relevant information in Uber’s documentation, uses a language model to explain that information, and gives engineers a way to continue the conversation or ask a human for help.

The interesting part about Genie is how Uber has connected multiple capabilities into building a working support system that fits seamlessly into an engineer’s workflow.

In this article, we will understand how Genie prepares knowledge, retrieves it, and generates answers. Here’s what we will cover:

  • The problem that Genie is trying to solve

  • What does Genie do?

  • How Genie gains knowledge

  • How Genie finds specific information from that knowledge

  • How Genie handles user questions

  • What does a typical Genie workflow look like

  • How Genie makes sure the answer is correct

  • What if Genie isn’t able to answer something

  • How Genie collects feedback

  • How Uber evaluates Genie’s performance

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

The Problem Genie Is Trying to Solve

The problem starts with how engineering teams support one another.

In a large software-driven company, many teams build platforms that other developers use to perform their jobs. A platform might provide tools for various activities such as software deployment, data processing, or working with ML workflows. Developers from other teams making use of these platforms inevitably need help with configuration, errors, or understanding unfamiliar features.

In a typical setup, the team responsible for managing a platform assigns an engineer to handle incoming issues during a particular period. This responsibility is commonly about providing on-call support. Although on-call work can definitely involve urgent production incidents, the problem Genie is trying to solve is geared towards everyday tech support that developers on platform teams provide through Slack channels.

For example, a developer from a product team might ask how to configure a platform feature. The on-call engineer reads the question and requests more details. The person asking responds, then waits again. Eventually, the on-call engineer identifies the relevant documentation or explains the required steps. Even a relatively straightforward question can involve several rounds of back-and-forth conversation and waiting.

Uber reports that its internal support channels received approximately 45K questions each month. At that volume, repeated questions consume considerable engineering time that the platform teams could utilize for better stuff.

Much of the information needed to answer such questions already exists somewhere. However, it is often scattered across Engwiki, which is Uber’s internal engineering wiki, or its internal Stack Overflow, and other documents. Finding the right information becomes difficult enough that it is much easier to ask another person.

Genie is designed to make that existing knowledge available through the Slack channels where developers already ask for help.

What does Genie do?

Genie combines finding information with explaining it.

A large language model (LLM) can produce readable explanations and answer technical questions. However, its general training doesn’t automatically give it knowledge of Uber’s private platforms, internal procedures, or documentation.

Therefore, Uber needed a way to connect a language model to its internal knowledge base. Two approaches help with this: fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

Fine-tuning means further training an existing model using examples selected for a particular purpose. Uber explains that this approach would require a collection of high-quality, varied training examples, along with sufficient computing resources to update the base model as new examples come up.

On the other hand, RAG supplies relevant information when a question is asked. The system first searches a knowledge collection, retrieves useful passages, and then gives those passages to the LLM along with the question. The model uses all this information to generate its answer.

For example, suppose a developer asks how to change a setting in an internal platform. A RAG system searches the platform’s documentation, finds the passage explaining that setting, and gives it to the model. The model turns the retrieved information into a response appropriate to the question.

Uber chose RAG for Genie because it could begin with existing documentation and be ready for launch sooner without the need to first assemble a fine-tuning dataset. This still needed a lot of work to collect, prepare, and evaluate the documentation. It also meant that updating the external knowledge collection could improve the information available to Genie without retraining the model for every change in documentation.

How Genie Gains the Required Knowledge

Preparing knowledge happens separately from answering questions. Before Genie can retrieve useful information, Uber must turn its scattered documents into a searchable collection. This preparation happens using an ETL pipeline.

ETL stands for extract, transform, and load.

  • Extraction means fetching content from internal sources.

  • Transformation means preparing that content for retrieval, including breaking it into pieces and generating numerical representations.

  • Loading means making the resulting data available to the search infrastructure.

Uber engineering team uses Apache Spark to run this work. For reference, Spark is a system for processing data across multiple workers, allowing a large preparation job to be divided into smaller pieces of work.

The pipeline fetches content through interfaces provided by sources such as Engwiki and Uber’s internal Stack Overflow. It places the results into a Spark DataFrame. Think of it as a table with rows and columns.

At this stage, a row contains information such as the document’s source URL, its text, and additional metadata. Here, metadata is information that describes the document rather than the content of that document.

Keeping the source URL alongside the text is important throughout the system. This is because Genie needs to eventually connect an answer back to the real documentation that supports it. Preserving this relationship during the preparation phase makes it easy to perform source attribution later on.

How Genie Finds Specific Information

Embeddings allow Genie to search for related meaning within its knowledge base. Once Uber has collected all the documentation, the next challenge is finding the passages that relate to a user’s question.

The system first divides documents into smaller pieces called chunks. For example, a long document might contain installation instructions, configuration options, and troubleshooting guidance. However, a question about one configuration option may only need a small part of that document. Chunking makes those smaller passages available as individual retrieval candidates.

Uber uses LangChain to chunk its wiki content. It then uses an OpenAI embedding model to generate an embedding for each chunk. An embedding is a list of numbers that represents aspects of a piece of text’s meaning. An embedding model is designed so that related texts have representations that can be found through similarity search. This helps a system find relevant information even when a question and a document use different wording. For example, a question might refer to a job “taking too long,” while a relevant document discusses an “execution time limit.” These phrases are just examples, but they show why searching for related meaning can be a game-changer when exact keywords differ.

The resulting data keeps each chunk associated with its embedding and source information. The original text still remains essential. The embedding simply helps the search system locate a passage. The passage itself supplies information for the language model to read.

Uber generates embeddings using custom Python functions executed through Spark. This lets embedding generation fit into the same data-processing pipeline as document collection and preparation.

How Genie Handles User Questions

Uber prepares the search infrastructure to serve questions. Creating embeddings produces searchable data, but that data still has to reach the systems that handle live requests. This is handled through the Pusher stage.

Two internal systems are used here:

  • Sia: This is Uber’s internal vector database solution. A vector database supports searching numerical representations such as embeddings.

  • Terrablob: This is Uber’s blob storage, which holds stored data and files used by the pipeline and serving infrastructure.

A bootstrap job ingests data into Sia, followed by Spark jobs that build and merge an index that organizes data for efficient searching.

The resulting index data is stored in Terrablob. Serving machines, called leaves, download the base index and synchronize snapshot data. These leaves handle searches against the loaded index when requests arrive.

This separates the work of building searchable knowledge from the work of answering an individual question.

  • Document preparation and index construction happen through the ingestion pipeline.

  • Live requests use the index made available to the serving machines.

What Does a Typical Genie Workflow Look Like

Each incoming question goes through retrieval before generation. Once the knowledge collection is ready, Genie can answer questions. The central backend component for this is Uber’s Knowledge Service.

Here’s how it works:

  • When someone posts a question in Slack, the Genie bot sends it to Knowledge Service. The service converts that question into an embedding.

  • It then searches the vector database for document chunks with related embeddings.

  • The search returns relevant passages associated with their source information. Those passages become part of the material sent to the LLM, together with the user’s question and instructions for answering.

  • Next, the model generates a response, which is returned through Genie to Slack.

There are two distinct model responsibilities in this flow.

The embedding model produces numerical representations that support retrieval. On the other hand, the LLM reads the retrieved text and produces the written response.

This difference is useful when dealing with failures. Genie might retrieve unsuitable passages, or it might retrieve useful passages and still generate an inadequate answer. Improving the system requires checking both stages.

How Genie Makes Sure the Answer is Correct

Uber gives the model explicit boundaries for generating its answers. An LLM can generate a plausible statement that is incorrect or unsupported. This behavior is commonly called hallucination. In an internal support system, an invented instruction could send a developer in the wrong direction.

Uber addresses this partly through how it constructs the model’s input.

Each retrieved result is presented as a separate sub-context, together with its source URL. A sub-context is simply a clearly identified piece of supporting material within the larger prompt. The model is instructed to answer using the provided sub-contexts and to provide source URLs as citations. This gives it explicit evidence to work from and gives the user a way to check the supporting documentation. For example, if several passages discuss different parts of a configuration process, preserving each passage’s source helps the generated explanation remain traceable to the actual source.

These measures reduce the risk of unsupported answers, but a source link doesn’t guarantee that every statement is correct. The retrieved passage must be relevant, the underlying document must be accurate, and the model must represent it faithfully. This is why evaluation remains an essential part of the architecture.

Uber also restricts the knowledge available to Genie. The team preselects sources that are broadly available to Uber developers because some internal information would be inappropriate to expose through model processing or Slack responses.

What if Genie Isn’t Able to Answer Something

The conversation includes a clear path to human support. A support interaction often continues after the first answer. Someone may need clarification, discover that the suggested information doesn’t quite address their situation, or require an action that documentation cannot provide.

Uber redesigned Genie’s interaction flow to deal with these possibilities. Its responses include action buttons that let users ask a follow-up question, mark the issue as resolved, or contact human support.

If Genie lacks enough information to answer, it tells the user and directs them to the on-call developers responsible for the platform. When a user escalates an interaction to human support, the human developer takes over while Genie stays muted. This keeps the conversation focused while an engineer handles the issue.

This feature is really important because successful support involves more than producing a paragraph of text. The user needs to understand what to do next. An answer that helps only partially can still be valuable if it leads smoothly into clarification or human assistance.

How Genie Collects Feedback

User feedback measures the impact of the answer. Uber collects feedback directly in Slack, where users can select a response category.

  • Resolved: The answer completely resolved the issue.

  • Helpful: The answer provided some help, but more assistance is needed.

  • Not Helpful: The answer was wrong or didn’t address the question.

  • Not Relevant: The request requires human help that Genie cannot provide, such as a code review.

The differentiation between these categories is very important. Partial help differs from complete resolution. Similarly, an incorrect answer differs from a request that falls outside what a documentation assistant can accomplish.

When a user submits feedback, a Slack plugin collects it together with relevant metadata. It sends that information through a Kafka topic, which acts as a stream of events, into a Hive table, where it can be stored and analyzed in the future. Uber then displays the resulting metrics in a dashboard.

This creates a record of how Genie performs in real use. Without such a record, a system could answer many questions while its operators had little visibility into whether those answers actually helped anyone.

How Uber Evaluates the Performance of Genie

Uber evaluates both the answers and the documents behind them. User feedback provides direct evidence of Genie’s usefulness. However, Uber also supports custom evaluations of qualities such as hallucination and answer relevance.

For these evaluations, a separate pipeline retrieves Genie’s recorded context and responses from Hive. It combines them with relevant information such as Slack metadata and user feedback, then prepares the data for an evaluator.

The evaluator uses an “LLM as a judge” approach. This means a language model receives an evaluation prompt that tells it how to assess the material. Its task is to examine an existing answer against the chosen criteria. For example, an evaluation prompt could ask whether an answer addresses the question and whether its claims are supported by the supplied context.

The evaluation results are processed into metrics and published in a report available through the interface. Uber says these evaluations can help plan improvements to both retrieval and generation steps.

The evaluation can also extend to the source documents themselves. This is a particularly useful part of the design because answer quality depends on the material available for retrieval. If a document is unclear, incomplete, or inaccurate, retrieving it successfully may still produce a poor support experience.

Uber’s document evaluation pipeline represents each document as a row in a Spark dataframe. It sends the document and a custom evaluation prompt to an LLM judge. The model returns a score, an explanation of that score, and actionable suggestions for improving the document. These results are published in a report that is also accessible through the Michelangelo interface. For example, a document might describe a procedure while leaving prerequisites unclear. Improving that document can give Genie better material to retrieve and explain, while also helping developers who read the documentation directly.

To summarize, the two evaluation processes examine different parts of the system. Answer evaluation checks what Genie produces in a particular interaction. Document evaluation checks the quality of the knowledge from which future answers will be constructed.

Conclusion

Genie was launched in September 2023. Within a year, Uber reported 154 Slack channels using Genie. More than 70K questions were answered during this time. The overall helpfulness rate was 48.9%, which is like a full-resolution rate, with engineering time savings of around 13000 hours.

This cost tracking is generated by following calls through the system. Running a model-backed service across many support channels also requires visibility into its costs. Uber provides that visibility by carrying an identifier through the request flow.

When a Slack client or another platform calls Knowledge Service, it passes a UUID. Knowledge Service forwards this identifier in request metadata to Michelangelo Gateway. The identifier can be included in an audit log and used to track costs associated with it.

Genie is a cutting-edge bot with the goal of streamlining on-call management, optimizing incident response, and improving team collaboration. It has the potential to change the entire experience of how users and on-call developers of any platform interact and engage within the respective platform’s Slack channel.
